title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows. Operational deployment requires evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to live networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited.

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this question as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an interpretation of ceiling effects grounded in archived artifacts; and (5) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research spans intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, RCA, and early agentic automation proposals. Several recent surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[2],[5].

Generate→validate→repair architectures are proposed across domains (NetOps, program repair, DevOps); some domain‑specific studies (notably in automated program repair and tool‑assisted DevOps prototypes) report improved repair rates or reduced unsafe commits under narrow datasets and particular validators, but these findings are context dependent and do not constitute broad operational validation for NetOps change execution [6],[7]. In short, the literature motivates validator‑coupled pipelines but also highlights that empirical gains depend on task bank construction, validator coverage, and experimental design; large‑scale, reproducible, paired evaluations that isolate verifier/gate effects for intent→configuration NetOps workflows remain scarce.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1. The preregistration fixed: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate; model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1); deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy; repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These items and parameter values were frozen before observing outputs and are archived in the execution and preregistration artifacts.

Generation semantics clarification. The executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent; therefore the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that same first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance.

Model and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded in the execution manifest). Model configuration recorded that max_output_tokens=2000 and maximum_attempts_per_call=1. Crucially, the run recorded temperature=null in the model configuration; null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic model sampling (it does not imply temperature=0), and no claim of deterministic sampling is made. The adapter produced exactly one sampled generation per pair which was reused under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Task bank and sampling. A deterministic task generator produced intent→configuration items with embedded workflow policies (sequence constraints, protected interfaces, group availability constraints). The preregistered deterministic sampler selected 200 paired intents by a fixed index rule; selection was outcome‑independent. Tasks include explicit required_sequence lists used to assess sequencing and precondition correctness. Difficulty metadata was recorded per task to enable exploratory stratified inspection.

Validator, gating, and scoring. The deterministic validator implemented sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group/minimum_up constraints, and reachability/policy consistency checks appropriate for the canonical emulated topologies. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization; scoring returned reason codes (e.g., VALID_CONFIGURATION) and violation codes when present. Guarded episodes permitted up to one automated repair attempt per preregistered budget; repair attempts and their traces were archived when used.

Confirmatory analysis. The preregistered primary analysis used a paired binary test (McNemar‑equivalent) implemented by the analysis executor and reported discordant pair counts, an exact two‑sided p‑value, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Missingness policy and retry rules were preregistered; the run produced no retriable infrastructure failures.
sections.results:
Execution accounting summary. The run executed as preregistered. One shared initial generation was produced per pair (200 model calls total) under shared_initial_candidate semantics; no provider or infrastructure retries occurred and no episodes were dropped. The guarded pipeline executed deterministic validation for each shared candidate and allowed at most one automated repair attempt per the preregistered budget.

Primary confirmatory results. The paired contingency table of unsafe_flag outcomes across 200 pairs is fully concordant: n11=200 (valid in both arms), n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Consequently the paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0, the exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0, and the paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). The zero‑width CI and p = 1.0 follow directly from the absence of discordant pairs under the preregistered estimand.

Repair activity and diagnostics. No automated repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_applied = false for all guarded traces). Representative episodes show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and validator final_state snapshots consistent with the reference expected states; violation_count = 0 for all episodes examined. These diagnostics indicate that, for the chosen model, prompt family, and synthetic task bank, sampled first‑pass candidates satisfied the validator's rule set.

Missingness and contamination. The run produced complete_pair_count = 200 with zero failed or unscorable episodes and no contamination flags under the preregistered detection rules. Deterministic reconciliation and provider audits confirmed episode accounting consistency.

Latency. Because only a single model call was required per pair under shared_initial_candidate semantics, total model call accounting equals 200. The guarded arm incurred deterministic validator execution time but no repair cycles; archived timing artifacts record per‑pair validation latency distributions for reproducibility and follow‑up planning.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing complete concordance (n11 = 200) implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, and the validator ruleset, the sampled initial candidates met the validator constraints. The archived analysis artifacts reproduce this outcome exactly.

Why the result is not a general refutation of validator value. The null is specific to the execution design: (1) task‑bank alignment—tasks were synthesized with required_sequences that closely matched the expected prompt schema and thus increased the chance of correct syntactic mappings; (2) validator coverage—validator rules encoded sequencing and precondition checks that aligned with the reference synthesis; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance that might generate discordant outcomes. All three contributors are traceable in the preregistration and execution metadata.

Design recommendations. To obtain nondegenerate inference about verifier/gate value we recommend preregistered modifications that are directly implementable using the archived artifacts: (a) inject adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates; (b) adopt an independent‑generation per‑condition design (two independent model calls per pair) to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model variance (this increases model_call budget accordingly); (c) evaluate multiple model versions or sampling settings to expose sampling variance effects; and (d) expand the repair budget or enable iterative repair loops when initial violations are nontrivial. These recommendations derive from comparing the current artifacts to the preregistered estimand semantics and execution accounting.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate choice intentionally restricts the estimand to validator/gate effects on identical first passes; it eliminates sampling variance but also limits generality. Construct validity: the unsafe_flag depends on validator rule coverage and may omit vendor‑specific side effects outside those rules. External validity: results use a single model and synthetic tasks, so transfer to other models, real topologies, or live devices is limited. Conclusion validity: the study was powered for a preregistered detectable effect (~10 percentage points) but observed a ceiling effect; hence the null does not rule out verifier benefits under different sampling or adversarial conditions.

Reproducibility and artifact availability. All core artifacts (preregistration, task manifest, model configuration, per‑episode responses, validator traces, and analysis outputs) are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement; researchers can replay the exact run under the same adapter or modify the archived task seeds and generation semantics to implement the recommended follow‑ups.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the deterministic validator, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics. It does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., adversarial inputs, independent per‑condition generation, multiple model samples). We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

Models and tools: single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration/adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Human role and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topical family and constrained the initial prompt pre‑lock; all literature review, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review emulation, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the lock. Generation semantics clarification: the executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task manifest is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
